title: Garmin CIRQA Launches at $199 With No Forced Subscription
excerpt: Garmin's first screen-free band, the CIRQA, is on sale at $199 and takes direct aim at Whoop's mandatory monthly fee. Here's what buyers should know.
body:
Garmin just put a $199.99 screen-free band on shelves that does the one thing Whoop refuses to: it works without a monthly bill. The CIRQA went on sale July 24, and for anyone who has eyed a recovery-focused wearable but balked at renting it forever, that's the headline.

The CIRQA is Garmin's first band with no screen at all. It reads your body around the clock and sends everything to the Garmin Connect app on your phone, rather than lighting up on your wrist. That puts it squarely against Whoop, the band that popularized the screenless, subscription-first model. The difference is the price tag actually buys you the hardware.

## Garmin CIRQA: What the $199 Band Actually Does

Garmin announced the CIRQA on July 21 and made it available to buy from July 24 at $199.99 in the US, £179.99 in the UK, and €199.99 in Europe. It's on Garmin.com and Amazon now.

The band tracks wrist-based heart rate, Garmin's Body Battery energy score, Pulse Ox, stress, skin temperature, and sleep continuously. It auto-detects more than 80 activities, so a walk or a workout logs itself without you tapping anything. Battery life is rated up to 10 days per charge, which is roughly a week longer than most smartwatches and in the same league as Whoop's multi-day runtime.

The subscription question has a real answer, and it has a footnote. Core metrics, heart rate, sleep, Body Battery, stress, and the activity tracking, are free in Garmin Connect with no fee ever. That's the whole point of the product. Garmin does sell an optional Connect+ tier at $6.99 a month or $69.99 a year for extras like guided strength plans, nutrition tracking, and its Active Intelligence AI features. The band you buy is fully functional without paying Garmin another cent.

## What It Means for Buyers

Compare that to Whoop, where the band is effectively free but useless without an ongoing membership. Cancel the plan and the hardware stops. Buy a CIRQA, cancel nothing, and it keeps tracking your recovery for the life of the device. Over two years, that gap is hundreds of dollars.

The winners here are people who want continuous recovery and sleep data but hate the rental model, and existing Garmin owners whose watch data will pool into the same Connect app and Body Battery score. If you already trust Garmin's sleep and stress numbers from a watch, the CIRQA is the low-profile, all-day companion that fills the gaps when the watch is off the charger.

Who should ignore it? Anyone who wants a screen. This band shows you nothing on your wrist. No time, no notifications, no glanceable stats. If you want a display and structured training tools, a proper watch is the better spend, and our [Garmin Forerunner 165 review](/posts/garmin-forerunner-165-review) covers the runner-first option that still skips a mandatory subscription. The CIRQA is a data-collection tool, not a watch replacement.

It also lands on a theme worth watching. Between Garmin refusing to gate core metrics and the steady buyer backlash against fee-locked features, the pressure on "buy the hardware, then rent the software" is building. The CIRQA is Garmin planting a flag on the side of one-time payment.

## Buy or Wait?

If you specifically want a screenless recovery band and you've been holding off on Whoop because of the subscription, buy now. At $199.99 with free core tracking and a 10-day battery, the CIRQA is the most buyer-friendly version of this category to date, and there's no launch-window penalty since it's already at its standard price on Garmin.com and Amazon.

Wait only if you're not sure you want a screen-free device. This is a brand-new product line, so first-batch owner feedback on daily accuracy and app reliability is still thin. If a display matters to you at all, put the $199 toward a Garmin watch instead. For everyone else who's been priced out by monthly fees, the CIRQA is the clearest reason yet to stop renting your wearable.

title: Blink Outdoor 4 Review: The Cheap Cam's Hidden Cost
excerpt: Our Blink Outdoor 4 review breaks down the two-year battery, the subscription catch, and whether the cheapest outdoor cam is actually cheap.
body:
A $40 outdoor security camera sounds too good to argue with. Then you go to save a clip of the package thief, and Blink asks for your credit card. That is the part nobody mentions when the Blink Outdoor 4 shows up in a weekend deal roundup, and it is the whole reason this review exists.

The Outdoor 4 is one of the best-selling wireless cameras on Amazon, and its sticker price swings hard. A single camera has dropped to roughly $38 on a good sale and sits closer to $100 at list. So the real question isn't whether it's cheap. It's what "cheap" actually costs you once the camera is on the wall.

---

## What Is the Blink Outdoor 4?

The Blink Outdoor 4 is the fourth-generation wireless outdoor camera from Blink, the Amazon-owned brand built around low prices and long battery life. It shoots 1080p HD video with a 143-degree field of view, adds two-way talk, and uses infrared for black-and-white night vision. It's weather-resistant, so it handles rain and heat on a porch or driveway without a cover.

The headline feature is power. Two AA lithium batteries run the camera for up to two years before you swap them, according to Blink. There's no wire to run, no charging cable dangling down the siding. The 1-camera kit includes a Sync Module Core, the small hub that connects the camera to your Wi-Fi.

Setup is the other strength. Owners consistently report getting a camera live in under ten minutes through the Blink app: scan a code, pick a spot, done. For anyone who has fought with a fussy smart-home device, that matters.

---

## Who Should Buy the Blink Outdoor 4?

This camera is for the renter or homeowner who wants a simple deterrent and a record of who came to the door, without running wires or paying a security company. If your goal is "let me glance at the driveway and get a ping when something moves," the Outdoor 4 does that cheaply and reliably.

It's also a good pick if you're already in Amazon's ecosystem. The camera ties into Alexa, so you can pull up the feed on an Echo Show with your voice. If you own other Blink or Ring gear, a single app handles the lot.

It's the wrong camera for anyone who wants sharp faces at distance or fine detail after dark. 1080p is fine for "a person is at the door" and weak for "read the license plate across the street." Owner photos back that up: usable, not forensic. If detail is the point, look higher up the range.

---

## What the Blink Outdoor 4 Gets Right

Three things make this camera punch above its price, and one thing quietly complicates the value.

- **Two-year battery life.** The AA lithium setup is the real headline. Most competitors need a recharge every few months. Blink owners genuinely report going a year-plus between swaps, which turns the camera into a mount-and-forget device.
- **Dead-simple setup and app.** The Blink app is one of the least frustrating in this category. Adding a camera, setting motion zones, and sharing access with family all take minutes, not an evening.
- **It's cheap, and it goes cheaper.** At list it's an easy budget pick. On sale it becomes an impulse buy, which is exactly why bundles keep landing in deal roundups.
- **Free local storage, with an asterisk.** Blink supports saving clips to a USB drive at no monthly cost. The catch: that needs a Sync Module 2, not the Sync Module Core included in this kit. So "free local storage" is real, but it may cost you a separate hub first.

---

## What You'll Actually Pay

The price you see is rarely the price you pay over time. As a piece of hardware, the Outdoor 4 is priced right where a budget cam should be, and the tracked price widget above shows where today's number sits against its history, so you can tell a genuine clearance dip from the everyday price.

Then there's the recurring math. To get person detection, saved cloud clips, and the smarter alerts most buyers assume are included, you need a Blink Subscription after the 30-day trial ends. That runs $3.99 a month per device on the Basic plan, or $11.99 a month for unlimited cameras on Plus. Buy one camera on a $40 sale, add Basic, and you've matched the sticker price in under a year of fees. That isn't a scam, plenty of people happily pay it, but it changes what "the cheap camera" means.

---

## Blink Outdoor 4 vs. the No-Fee Alternatives

The honest comparison here is about ongoing cost, not just megapixels.

If a monthly fee is a dealbreaker and you can point the camera indoors, our [eufy Indoor Cam E30 review](/posts/eufy-indoor-cam-e30-review-4k-without-the-monthly-fee) is the counterpoint: sharper 4K video and local storage with no subscription at all. It won't survive a rainstorm on the porch, but for a doorway, hallway, or nursery it delivers more detail for zero recurring cost.

If your real target is the front door and you want a video doorbell instead of a wall cam, our [Ring Battery Doorbell (2nd gen) review](/posts/ring-battery-doorbell-2nd-gen-review-2k-on-a-budget) covers the other Amazon-family option. It shares Blink's subscription model, so the fee math is similar, but head-on 2K coverage of a doorway is a better fit for package-watching than a wide 1080p field.

Blink wins when you need battery-powered outdoor coverage on a budget and don't mind either paying the fee or adding a Sync Module 2 for local clips.

---

## The Subscription Catch

Here's the one thing to sit with before you buy. The features that make a security camera feel smart, person detection and saved clips you can pull up later, are the exact features gated behind the subscription. Without it, motion alerts and live view still work, but you can't reliably go back and watch what happened after the fact unless you've set up local storage on a Sync Module 2.

Owner reviews reflect this. The one-star complaints rarely fault the hardware. They fault the surprise of learning that "save this clip" requires a plan. Go in expecting that, and the Outdoor 4 is a fair deal. Go in expecting a $40 camera to do everything for free, and you'll feel misled.

---

## Blink Outdoor 4 FAQ

**Q: Does the Blink Outdoor 4 require a subscription?**
No for the basics, yes for the good parts. Live view, motion alerts, and two-way talk work without a plan. Person detection and saved cloud clips need a Blink Subscription after the 30-day trial, or you can add a Sync Module 2 and save clips to a USB drive for free.

**Q: How long does the Blink Outdoor 4 battery last?**
Blink rates the two AA lithium batteries for up to two years of typical use, and owners generally report a year or more before swapping. Heavy motion traffic and lots of live-view sessions drain them faster, so a busy driveway won't hit the full two years.

**Q: Can the Blink Outdoor 4 store video locally without a fee?**
Yes, but not with the hub in this box. Local USB storage needs a Sync Module 2. The Sync Module Core included in the 1-camera kit connects the camera to Wi-Fi but does not support a USB drive, so budget for the upgrade if avoiding the subscription is the goal.

---

## The Verdict

The Blink Outdoor 4 is a genuinely good budget camera as long as you know the sticker isn't the whole bill. Buy it if you want simple, battery-powered outdoor coverage and you've decided how you'll handle clip storage, either paying the fee or adding a Sync Module 2.

---

If the price in the card above is sitting near one of its sale lows, and you're clear-eyed about the subscription, this is an easy pick for the money.
